passage:
Outside the exam hall, Shankar noticed Gurpreet on the bench, twisting her hands round and round as if wringing out a wet cloth. Scared of the maths paper, he guessed. He sat beside her. "You know fractions better than me. You'll be fine."

Gurpreet gave a small smile. "It's not the paper. My little brother had a fever all night, and Mummy took him to the clinic this morning. I keep thinking about him."

Shankar was quiet for a moment. Then he offered her a piece of his jaggery. "Maybe ask the office if you can phone home at lunch?"

Her hands went still.

qa.q: Where did Mummy take Gurpreet's little brother that morning?
qa.a: To the clinic.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet worried about as she wrung her hands?
qa.a: She was anxious about her little brother, who had a fever all night, not mainly about the maths paper as Shankar had guessed.

qa.q: What did Shankar do that helped, even though his guess was wrong?
qa.a: He sat beside her with a friendly word, which gave her a chance to share the real worry, and then suggested phoning home at lunch.

qa.q: How did Shankar read the hand-wringing at first?
qa.a: Shankar took it as fear of the maths paper, and learned that the same signal can come from a different worry.

grounding: It shows a child reading a classmate's hand-wringing before a test as nervousness, offering a friendly word, and learning the cause was different.

passage:
The whole village was at the boat race on the backwaters, and Jahnavi wanted a photo with Joseph, who was visiting from Manchester for the summer. She grinned into the phone camera and held up two fingers, the back of her hand facing out.

Joseph laughed, then winced. "Er, don't do that one at my school. That way round it's rude in Britain, like a really bad word."

Jahnavi snatched her hand down. "Here it means victory! Or peace!"

"I know. Palm facing out is fine there too."

She turned her hand around. Then she gave a big thumbs-up. "And this?"

"That one's been good everywhere I've been."

qa.q: Where was Joseph visiting from?
qa.a: From Manchester, for the summer.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel when Joseph said her V-sign was rude in Britain?
qa.a: Embarrassed and a little defensive; she snatched her hand down and insisted it means victory or peace here.

qa.q: What is a wise habit for Jahnavi when making friends from other places?
qa.a: Ask what a gesture means where they come from, or check before using it in photos or when travelling.

qa.q: How might Joseph feel about correcting Jahnavi?
qa.a: Joseph seems a bit awkward, laughing then wincing, but wants to save her from being misunderstood rather than to shame her.

grounding: It shows a child learning that a V-sign that means victory at home is rude the other way round in Britain, while a thumbs-up travels better.

passage:
When Nani arrived at the flat in Oslo, straight from the airport in her thick shawl, Amara bent and touched both of Nani's feet. Nani placed a hand on her head. "Jeete raho, my girl."

Lars, from next door, stared from the doorway. "Why do you touch her shoes?"

"It's respect," Amara said, "and she gives me a blessing back."

Amara's little cousin Pihu hid behind the sofa, shy of this new grandmother. "Pihu, touch Nani's feet," someone said. Amara's mother shook her head. "Only if she wants to. A namaste is respect too."

Pihu waved instead. Nani waved back, delighted. Lars shyly held out his hand, and Nani shook it.

qa.q: What did Nani place on Amara's head?
qa.a: Nani placed a hand on her head.

qa.q: What might Pihu have been feeling behind the sofa?
qa.a: Shy and a little uneasy with a grandmother she didn't know yet, which is why she hid and chose to wave instead.

qa.q: Which choice protected Pihu while still honouring Nani?
qa.a: Amara's mother said Pihu should only touch Nani's feet if she wanted to and that a namaste is respect too, so Pihu could greet her with a wave.

qa.q: How does Lars see the custom at first?
qa.a: Lars is puzzled and asks why Amara touches Nani's shoes; after Amara explains, he joins in his own way with a handshake.

grounding: It shows a child touching an elder's feet for respect and a blessing, while a younger child is not forced and greets her another way.

passage:
At debate club, Yash raced through his opening speech like a train without brakes. From the back, Mr Rao smiled and pressed both palms gently down through the air. Yash took a breath and slowed. The words started to land.

Later, in the rebuttal, the other team called his idea "childish", and Yash's voice climbed. "That's not even—"

Beside him, Zainab pressed her palms down too, but her eyebrows were pinched together and she was shaking her head a little. Yash stopped. Same hands, different message: not "slower" but "careful, you're losing it". He unclenched his fist and made his point quietly. Zainab let out her breath.

qa.q: What word did the other team use for Yash's idea?
qa.a: Childish.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling when she pressed her palms down with pinched eyebrows?
qa.a: Worried that Yash was losing his temper and might hurt their case; her shaking head backs it up, and her breath out shows relief when he calmed.

qa.q: How did Yash tell the two palm-down gestures apart?
qa.a: He read the faces that came with them: Mr Rao's smile meant "slow down", while Zainab's pinched eyebrows meant "careful, calm down".

qa.q: What would change if Mr Rao had made the gesture with an eye-roll?
qa.a: It might feel dismissive, like being told to shut up, and Yash could get flustered instead of slowing down.

grounding: It shows a child learning that the palms-down gesture means slow down from a teacher and worried calm down from a friend, read through face and tone.

subtype: Time-out gesture and pausing a game [Expressing]
passage:
I'm Salma, Jatin's classmate, and I was on the other team in Friday's kho-kho match. Halfway through, Deepak and Vinod started shoving over whether a foul counted. Jatin ran between them and made a T with his hands, flat palm on top of his fingers. "Time out! Let's ask Sir." Everyone froze. Sir explained the rule, and we played on.

Later, Rinku was about to be tagged, and suddenly he made a T too. "Time out! My lace!" His laces were perfectly tied. Everybody groaned, and even his own team shouted, "Play!"

I don't know what Jatin was thinking, but his T stopped a fight, and Rinku's just stopped the game.

qa.q: What did Rinku say was the problem?
qa.a: His lace, though his laces were perfectly tied.

qa.q: What might Jatin have been feeling when he ran between Deepak and Vinod?
qa.a: Probably worried that the shoving would turn into a real fight and keen to settle the rule fairly, though Salma can't know for sure.

qa.q: What made Jatin's time-out work where Rinku's failed?
qa.a: Jatin used it honestly to stop a quarrel and get help with a rule, while Rinku used it to dodge being tagged, and everyone could see his laces were tied.

qa.q: How did the other players see Rinku's time-out?
qa.a: They saw through it and felt annoyed, groaning and shouting "Play!", even his own team.

grounding: It is a classmate's account of one child using the time-out T honestly to stop a quarrel and another using it to dodge being tagged, which peers spot.

subtype: Reading a speaker's gestures for meaning [Interpreting]
passage: "Amandeep, you watch your science teacher's hands closely. Good. I, your Gautam Tauji, learned that the hard way. Our teacher in Class 6, Mr Bhatt, loved big gestures. One day he talked about dropping a stone and a feather. For the stone, his hand shot down like lightning. For the feather, his fingers floated side to side, slow as a leaf. So I wrote in my notebook: heavy things always fall faster. Something bothered me, though, and after class I asked, 'Sir, would a heavy stone and a small stone land together?' He stopped, then laughed. 'Yes! My hands made the feather too dramatic. It's the air that slows it.' Always ask, beta."

qa.q: What did young Gautam write in his notebook?
qa.a: Heavy things always fall faster.

qa.q: What was young Gautam feeling when something bothered him after class?
qa.a: Doubtful and curious, uneasy that the idea he got from the gestures might be wrong, which pushed him to ask.

qa.q: What choice in the story fixed the mistaken idea?
qa.a: Gautam's follow-up question, whether a heavy and a small stone would land together, made the teacher explain that it is the air that slows the feather.

qa.q: How did Mr Bhatt react to the question?
qa.a: He stopped, laughed and admitted his hands had made the feather too dramatic; he seems glad the question caught the mistake.

grounding: It is an elder's memory of a teacher's exaggerated gestures giving a wrong idea about falling objects, and a follow-up question checking the meaning.

passage:
Indu Didi had just started teaching at the new tuition centre in Kasaragod and had no idea where anything was. "Ishita, how do I get to your house for Sunday lunch?"

Ishita frowned. "You go… um…" Her words stuck. So her finger took over, drawing in the air: a long straight line past the temple, a big loop round the pond, then a sharp hook. "Left at the banyan tree! I forgot that till my hand did it."

Indu Didi traced the same path with her own finger, slowly, while Ishita watched. "Straight, round the pond, left at the banyan."

"Yes! And our gate is the blue one."

qa.q: What colour is Ishita's gate?
qa.a: The blue one.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel when her finger found the turn she had forgotten?
qa.a: Relieved and pleased 😊, as "Left at the banyan tree!" shows, after feeling stuck when the words wouldn't come.

qa.q: What did Indu Didi do that helped Ishita explain?
qa.a: She let Ishita gesture without hurrying her, then traced the same path back to check she had understood.

qa.q: What would change if Indu Didi had said, "Just tell me, don't wave your hands"?
qa.a: Ishita might have stayed stuck, since her hand was helping her remember the route, and Indu Didi would get worse directions.

grounding: It shows a child tracing a route in the air to give directions, the gesture helping her remember the turn, and an adult letting her gesture.

passage:
Wednesday

New school, day three. When Sarita Ma'am walks in, the whole class jumps up and says, "Good mooorning, Ma'am!" At my old school in Bengaluru we just stayed sitting and waved. On the first day I was the only one still in my chair, and my face went hot.

Today Ali, who came from Dubai last year, whispered, "Standing up feels like we're scared of her." I told him it's not scared, it's like when I touch Ajoba's feet before an exam. It's respect. He said at his house they kiss their grandfather's hand instead. So we worked out that everybody's respect looks different. I stood up fastest today!

Nilesh

qa.q: Where was Nilesh's old school?
qa.a: In Bengaluru.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel on the first day, as the only one still sitting?
qa.a: Embarrassed and out of place, as the hot face shows, since Nilesh did not yet know the new rule.

qa.q: What helped Nilesh and Ali understand each other's customs?
qa.a: They compared what respect looks like at home, touching Ajoba's feet and kissing a grandfather's hand, instead of judging each other's habits.

qa.q: How did Ali first see the class standing up?
qa.a: Ali felt it looked like being scared of the teacher, because it was not a custom he knew.

grounding: It is a child's diary about standing when a teacher enters and touching an elder's feet as respect, and learning that such customs differ between families and schools.

subtype: Slouching and sitting up in class [Interpreting]
passage: "Eshaan, sit however you like while you think. Let me, your Vidya Nani, tell you why. Thirty years ago I taught a boy called Mohan who slouched so low he was nearly under the desk. I was sure he was bored with my lessons, so I snapped at him in front of everyone: 'Sit up! This isn't your bed!' He sat up, went red and said nothing for a week. Then his mother came to see me. He had been helping at their dhaba until midnight every night. And you know what? Slouched in the next exam, he wrote the best essay in the class. I was wrong about him twice."

qa.q: Where had Mohan been helping until midnight?
qa.a: At their dhaba.

qa.q: What was Mohan likely feeling after Vidya snapped "Sit up!"?
qa.a: Embarrassed and hurt at being scolded in front of everyone; his reddening face and a week of silence show it.

qa.q: What choice in the story would have worked better than snapping?
qa.a: Vidya could have asked Mohan privately why he seemed so tired, instead of assuming the slouch meant boredom.

qa.q: How might Mohan's mother have felt coming to see the teacher?
qa.a: She likely felt worried for her son and wanted the teacher to understand that his tiredness came from late nights of work, not from boredom.

grounding: It is a retired teacher's memory of reading a pupil's slouch as boredom when it meant tiredness and, later, a comfortable way of thinking.

subtype: Pacing and fidgeting for energy or worry [Expressing]
passage:
The bus to the block science fair was late, and the kasba bus stand smelled of diesel and roasted peanuts. Swati couldn't sit. She paced from the tea stall to the timetable board and back, then sat and bounced her knee so hard the bench shook.

"Arre, beta, sit still!" said an old man beside her.

Mehak, holding their model of a water filter, watched her. "Scared or excited?"
"Both. And my legs just need to go."

Mehak stood up. "Then let's walk and practise our lines." Up and down they went, past the peanut cart, saying the steps aloud. By the tenth lap, Swati knew every word. Then the bus honked round the corner.

qa.q: What model was Mehak holding?
qa.a: Their model of a water filter.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling as she paced and bounced her knee?
qa.a: A mix of nervous and excited about the science fair, as she says herself, with energy that needed to move.

qa.q: Which choice helped Swati focus?
qa.a: Mehak turned the fidgeting into a walk while they practised their lines, so the movement helped Swati learn every word.

qa.q: How did the old man on the bench see Swati's bouncing?
qa.a: He saw it as restless fidgeting that should stop, not knowing it was her way of handling nerves and excitement.

grounding: It shows a child pacing and bouncing a leg before an event from nerves, excitement and energy, and a movement break helping her focus.
